root.stem: A 34-year-old man was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection 9 years ago. He took combination antiretroviral therapy for 6 years with an undetectable viral load, then stopped taking it 2 years ago. For 3 weeks he has had fever, severe watery diarrhea, fatigue and an 8-kg weight loss. White plaques on his tongue scrape off, leaving a red base, and the lymph nodes in his neck and armpits are enlarged. A modified acid-fast stain of his stool shows small round oocysts. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 90/mm3, his viral load is 100,000 copies/mL, and a chest x-ray shows diffuse hazy infiltrates in both lungs.
root.oneliner: 34M + HIV for 9 years, off antiretrovirals for 2 years + 3 weeks of fever, watery diarrhea, 8-kg weight loss + scrapable white tongue plaques + neck and axillary nodes + small acid-fast oocysts in stool + CD4+ count 90 + viral load 100,000 + diffuse hazy infiltrates in both lungs
highlight: White plaques on his tongue scrape off
diffuse hazy infiltrates in both lungs

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) due to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection
nodes.note: The retrovirus has destroyed so many CD4+ T cells that opportunistic infections have appeared. The clincher: **known HIV infection, off treatment, now with opportunistic infections, wasting and a very low CD4+ count**.

nodes.q: Which CD4+ T-lymphocyte count defines AIDS in a person with HIV?
nodes.note: A normal count is about 500 to 1500/mm3. An AIDS-defining illness (for example esophageal candidiasis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, chronic cryptosporidiosis or wasting) also counts, whatever the CD4+ count.

nodes.q: Which cell kills the HIV-infected CD4+ T cells and so lowers the count?
nodes.note: Cytotoxic T cells recognise viral peptides on the infected cell and destroy it. The virus itself also kills cells directly and fuses them into syncytia.

nodes.q: Besides helper T cells, which cell type carries the HIV genome in the tissues?
nodes.note: Macrophages and dendritic cells carry CD4 and the chemokine receptor CCR5, so the virus infects them and they act as a reservoir. Strains that use CXCR4 (another chemokine receptor) appear in late disease and target T cells. People homozygous for a CCR5 deletion are resistant to CCR5-using strains; maraviroc blocks CCR5. Not B cells, natural killer cells, neutrophils or endothelial cells.

nodes.q: His virus is not blocked by soluble CD4 (a decoy receptor). Which viral gene product has most likely mutated?
nodes.a: The envelope glycoprotein (gp120, encoded by the env gene)
nodes.note: Glycoprotein 120 (gp120) binds CD4 and then the coreceptor; glycoprotein 41 (gp41) drives fusion with the host membrane (enfuvirtide blocks gp41). Core, matrix, integrase and reverse transcriptase act inside the cell.

nodes.q: His genotype from his years on zidovudine shows a resistance mutation. Which virus-encoded enzyme carries it?
nodes.note: It is encoded by the pol gene, together with integrase and protease. Not thymidine kinase (the route to acyclovir resistance in herpes viruses). Copying RNA into DNA is the hallmark of retroviruses, so a drug that blocks a virus-encoded RNA-dependent DNA polymerase inhibits HIV, not herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, influenza virus or poliovirus.

nodes.q: How does zidovudine stop viral DNA synthesis?
nodes.a: It is a nucleoside analogue that lacks a 3' hydroxyl group, so it terminates the growing DNA chain
nodes.note: Tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine work the same way (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, NRTIs). Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside drug that binds the enzyme away from its active site and needs no phosphorylation.

nodes.q: His old regimen also included lopinavir boosted with ritonavir. Which step of viral replication do these drugs block?
nodes.a: Protein processing: cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein by the viral protease
nodes.note: Without cleavage the new virions stay immature and cannot infect, so resistance mutations arise in the protease gene. On the classic regimen of two reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus a protease inhibitor, failure mutations therefore sit in **reverse transcriptase and protease**. Ritonavir boosts the partner drug by inhibiting its breakdown (cytochrome P450 3A4). Not genome integration, uncoating or nucleic acid synthesis.

nodes.q: Which regimen is used to restart therapy?
nodes.a: Two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (for example tenofovir, emtricitabine and dolutegravir)
nodes.note: Do resistance genotyping first and choose active drugs by it. Therapy is lifelong and the aim is an undetectable viral load.

nodes.q: Two months into a new regimen, the viral load is undetectable and the CD4+ count has risen. What is the next step?
nodes.note: The regimen is working. Keep checking the viral load and CD4+ count at intervals; change drugs only for failure, toxicity or resistance.

nodes.q: Which fungus most likely causes his diffuse hazy lung infiltrates?
nodes.note: Cysts stain with silver stain and lactate dehydrogenase is high. It is a common AIDS-defining infection; untreated it ends in hypoxemic respiratory failure and death. A severe opportunistic infection with wasting and lymphopenia in a person not known to have HIV means **test for HIV**.

nodes.q: Once he recovers, which drug prevents this pneumonia from returning until his CD4+ count recovers on treatment?
nodes.note: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole also covers Toxoplasma. It is stopped once the CD4+ count stays above the AIDS threshold for 3 months on antiretroviral therapy.

nodes.q: Which organism causes the white plaques that scrape off his tongue?
nodes.note: Oral thrush is common as the CD4+ count falls. Extension to the esophagus (esophageal candidiasis) is an AIDS-defining illness.

nodes.q: Which protozoan causes his watery diarrhea?
nodes.note: Small round acid-fast oocysts in stool. Spread by oocysts in water that resist chlorine. In AIDS the diarrhea is profuse and long-lasting; it improves as the CD4+ count recovers on antiretroviral therapy.

nodes.q: His diarrhea does not improve with loperamide or other oral drugs. A stable injectable analogue of which natural hormone can stop it?
nodes.note: Somatostatin lowers intestinal secretion and slows gut motility.

nodes.q: He was treated for tuberculosis 4 months ago, yet a tuberculin skin test placed this week shows no induration. Which finding in his blood explains this?
nodes.a: Lymphocytopenia: too few CD4+ T cells to mount the delayed-type (type IV) reaction
nodes.note: This failure to react to skin-test antigens is called anergy. A negative test does not exclude tuberculosis in advanced HIV.

nodes.q: Which virus drives the brain lymphoma that AIDS patients are at greatest risk of?
nodes.note: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, an AIDS-defining cancer seen at CD4+ counts below 50/mm3. Kaposi sarcoma comes from human herpesvirus 8 and invasive cervical cancer from human papillomavirus.

nodes.q: Years before his diagnosis he had a painful genital ulcer with tender groin nodes. Which gram-negative coccobacillus causes such an ulcer and raised his risk of acquiring HIV?
nodes.note: Chancroid. Genital ulcers break the mucosal barrier and bring CD4+ cells to the surface, so HIV passes more easily; syphilis and genital herpes act the same way. Candida, Cryptococcus and cytomegalovirus do not raise the risk of acquiring HIV.

nodes.q: His hazy lung infiltrates could be cytomegalovirus pneumonitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: CD4+ count **below 50/mm3**; lung biopsy shows **owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions**; often with retinitis or colitis
CD4+ count **below 200/mm3**; **silver stain shows cysts**; high lactate dehydrogenase; responds to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

nodes.note: The trap: both give diffuse infiltrates and fever in advanced HIV.

nodes.q: His fever and diarrhea could come from other AIDS infections. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: Mycobacterium avium complex
**CD4+ count below 50/mm3; fever, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly; acid-fast bacilli in blood culture or in macrophages of the bowel wall**
His stool shows oocysts, not bacilli, and his count is 90
Cytomegalovirus colitis
**CD4+ count below 50/mm3; bloody diarrhea; colonic ulcers with owl's-eye inclusions**
His diarrhea is watery, not bloody
Cystoisospora belli infection
**Larger oval acid-fast oocysts; clears with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole**
His oocysts are small and round

root.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of fever, chills, sore throat, headache, diarrhea and a rash. She had unprotected sex with a new partner 4 weeks ago. Her throat is red with exudate, lymph nodes are enlarged in her neck, armpits and groin, and a red maculopapular rash covers her trunk and limbs. A rapid streptococcal antigen test and a heterophile antibody test are negative, and an HIV antibody test is negative. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 700/mm3 and her plasma HIV viral load is over 1 million copies/mL.
root.oneliner: 24F + 2 weeks of fever, sore throat, headache, diarrhea, maculopapular rash + new sexual partner + generalized adenopathy + negative strep and heterophile tests + negative HIV antibody + CD4+ 700 + viral load over 1 million
highlight: enlarged in her neck, armpits and groin

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks after exposure. The clincher: **fever, rash and diffuse adenopathy with a very high HIV viral load while the antibody test is still negative**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Acute retroviral syndrome (also called primary HIV infection)
nodes.note: All of these names describe the same illness.

nodes.q: Why is her HIV antibody test negative?
nodes.a: She has not yet seroconverted: antibodies appear weeks after infection (the window period)
nodes.note: Antibodies take about 3 to 12 weeks to appear. Viral RNA and a viral core antigen are detectable first, so her viral load is already very high and she is highly infectious.

nodes.q: Which viral antigen does a fourth-generation screening test detect before antibodies appear?
nodes.note: Encoded by the gag gene. The fourth-generation test combines p24 antigen with HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, which shortens the window period to about 2 to 3 weeks.

nodes.q: Besides CD4, which coreceptor do the strains that establish a new infection use?
nodes.note: Early (macrophage-tropic) strains use CCR5; strains that use CXCR4 emerge later and mark faster progression. Maraviroc blocks CCR5.

nodes.q: Which test confirms infection at this stage?
nodes.a: A plasma HIV RNA test (nucleic acid amplification)
nodes.note: A fourth-generation antigen and antibody test may also be positive. Repeat antibody testing later to document seroconversion.

nodes.q: When should antiretroviral therapy start?
nodes.a: As soon as the diagnosis is made
nodes.note: Early treatment shrinks the viral reservoir and prevents transmission once the viral load is undetectable. Counsel her and trace her partners.

nodes.q: Her fever, sore throat and nodes could suggest infectious mononucleosis. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both give fever, exudative pharyngitis and generalized adenopathy.

split.note: **Positive heterophile antibody test**, atypical lymphocytes, splenomegaly; a rash follows ampicillin
**Negative heterophile test + maculopapular rash + diarrhea + viral load over 1 million**

nodes.q: Other illnesses also cause fever, sore throat and nodes. Which finding in her case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: Late-stage AIDS
**Positive HIV antibody test + CD4+ count below 200/mm3 + opportunistic infections**
Her antibody test is negative and her CD4+ count is 700
HIV-2 infection
**West African link; slow course with a low viral load; antibody tests turn positive**
Her viral load is over 1 million
Streptococcal pharyngitis
**Positive rapid antigen test; tender neck nodes only; no rash or diarrhea**
Her strep test is negative and her nodes are generalized
Gonococcal pharyngitis
**Sore throat after oral sex with neck nodes only; positive culture or nucleic acid test**
Her nodes are generalized, with rash and diarrhea
Lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3)
**Painless genital ulcer, then a painful inguinal bubo**
No genital ulcer; her nodes are everywhere

root.stem: A 7-year-old boy from a rural area of Kentucky has had 2 weeks of cramping abdominal pain and diarrhea. Yesterday his mother found a pink, 20-cm worm that looked like an earthworm in his underwear. He often plays in mud with his bare hands and puts his fingers in his mouth, but he always wears shoes. He has had no fever, cough or blood-tinged sputum, and his stool has no visible blood. Examination is normal, and a blood count shows no anemia.
root.oneliner: 7M + 2 weeks of cramping abdominal pain and diarrhea + passed a pink 20-cm earthworm-like worm + plays in mud, hands to mouth, always wears shoes + no fever, cough or bloody sputum + no anemia
highlight: pink, 20-cm worm that looked like an earthworm
plays in mud with his bare hands
puts his fingers in his mouth
no fever, cough or blood-tinged sputum

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection with a large intestinal roundworm. The clincher: **a long, pink, earthworm-like worm passed in stool (or vomited) in a child who eats soil**.

nodes.q: The exam may name the organism rather than the disease. What is it?
nodes.note: The giant roundworm, the largest intestinal nematode in humans.

nodes.q: How did he acquire the infection?
nodes.a: By swallowing eggs from soil contaminated with human feces (fecal-oral route)
nodes.note: Eggs survive in warm moist soil for years. Not through the skin (hookworm, Strongyloides), not from puppies (Toxocara), and not from a black fly (Onchocerca), mosquito or tick bite.

nodes.q: After the eggs hatch in the gut, where do the larvae travel before the adult worm settles in the small intestine?
nodes.a: Through the blood to the lungs, up the airway and back down when swallowed
nodes.note: The lung passage can cause a transient cough and pneumonitis with eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome); he has no cough now.

nodes.q: Which finding on stool microscopy confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Fertilized eggs with a thick, bumpy (mamillated) shell
nodes.note: The worm itself, as in his case, also makes the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which acute abdominal emergency do heavy worm burdens cause in children?
nodes.a: Small bowel obstruction from a tangled mass of worms
nodes.note: It may lead to volvulus or perforation. Heavy infection also causes malnutrition and growth delay.

nodes.q: Which structure can a migrating adult worm block to cause colicky pain and jaundice?
nodes.note: Cholangitis, biliary colic or pancreatitis may follow.

nodes.q: Which drug treats it?
nodes.note: They bind beta-tubulin and stop microtubule formation in the worm. Pyrantel pamoate, which paralyses the worm, is the alternative and is preferred in pregnancy.

nodes.q: Playing in soil with abdominal pain and diarrhea could suggest hookworm. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both live in soil-contaminated areas and cause abdominal pain and diarrhea.

split.note: **Larvae penetrate the skin of bare feet**; blood loss gives **iron deficiency anemia**; no large worm in stool; thin-shelled eggs
**Swallowed eggs from soil + a large earthworm-like worm passed in stool**; no anemia

nodes.q: Other worms were possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: Enterobiasis (pinworm)
**Night-time perianal itching; a tiny white worm about 1 cm; eggs on a tape test**
No itching, and his worm is 20 cm long
Strongyloidiasis
**Larvae (not eggs) in stool after skin penetration; autoinfection; hyperinfection with steroids**
He always wears shoes

**Larvae migrate to the liver or eye after contact with puppy or kitten feces; high eosinophils; no adult worms in stool**

root.stem: A 6-month-old boy has had 10 days of cough that began with a low-grade fever, sneezing and a runny nose. The cough now comes in long rapid bursts that end with a loud gasp, and he sometimes vomits afterward. He has never received any vaccines, and he is afebrile between spells. His chest is clear. White blood cell count is 30,000/mm3 with 73% lymphocytes.
root.oneliner: 6-month-old M + 10 days of cough after a runny-nose prodrome + long rapid bursts ending in a gasp, post-cough vomiting + no vaccines + afebrile between spells + clear chest + WBC 30,000 with 73% lymphocytes
highlight: long rapid bursts that end with a loud gasp

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A prolonged cough illness of unvaccinated infants. The clincher: **paroxysms of cough ending in an inspiratory whoop + marked lymphocytosis**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called the 100-day cough, because it lasts weeks to months.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A small gram-negative coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium. It grows on Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe agar.

nodes.q: Which stage of the illness does the runny nose with low-grade fever represent?
nodes.note: It lasts 1 to 2 weeks and is the most contagious. The paroxysmal stage (weeks) follows, then the convalescent stage.

nodes.q: His white count is mostly lymphocytes. Which toxin causes the lymphocytosis?
nodes.note: It stops lymphocytes leaving the blood to enter tissues, so they pile up in the circulation. Because the lymphocytes are mature, this is not leukemia.

nodes.q: Pertussis toxin adds adenosine diphosphate-ribose to the inhibitory G protein (Gi) and switches it off. Neutrophil chemotaxis and oxidative killing are then impaired by increased activity of which enzyme?
nodes.note: With Gi off, adenylyl cyclase makes more cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The organism's own adenylate cyclase toxin adds to this. Not NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase, protein kinase C or phospholipase C.

nodes.q: Which product of the organism destroys the ciliated cells and causes the cough?
nodes.note: A fragment of its cell wall. Filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin help it stick to the cilia.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a nasopharyngeal swab
nodes.note: Culture is specific but is positive only early; serology is used in older patients.

nodes.q: Which antibiotic is given to him and to his household contacts?
nodes.note: A macrolide that blocks the 50S ribosome. It stops spread, but it shortens the cough only if started in the catarrhal stage. Hospitalize young infants.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening event may replace the whoop in young infants?
nodes.note: Other complications are pneumonia (the usual cause of death), seizures and encephalopathy.

nodes.q: Which vaccine would have prevented his illness?
nodes.a: Diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine (DTaP)
nodes.note: The pertussis part contains pertussis toxoid and adhesins. Given from 2 months of age. A booster (Tdap) is given to adolescents and to mothers in each pregnancy, to protect the newborn.

nodes.q: His cough and runny nose could suggest bronchiolitis from respiratory syncytial virus. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both start with a runny nose in an infant.

split.note: **Wheezing and crackles, fast breathing, low-grade fever**; normal or mildly raised white count
**Clear chest + paroxysmal coughing ending in a gasp + lymphocytosis**; unvaccinated

nodes.q: Other causes of cough in an infant were possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: Croup
**Barking cough with inspiratory stridor, hoarse voice; steeple sign on neck x-ray**
No bark or stridor; his voice is normal
Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia of infancy
**Age 1 to 3 months; staccato cough; eye discharge after birth; eosinophilia**
He is 6 months old with lymphocytosis and a clear chest
Foreign body aspiration
**Sudden choking in a toddler; one-sided wheeze or decreased breath sounds**

root.stem: A 6-year-old boy recently moved from a village in Niger. He has had repeated episodes of red, itchy, watery eyes for years, and flies gather around his face. His father and an uncle have similar eye symptoms and are now blind. Lifting his upper eyelid shows pale follicles on the inner surface and some scarring, and his eyelashes touch the eye. He has had no genital symptoms and was not born with eye discharge.
root.oneliner: 6M + recurrent red itchy eyes for years + from rural Niger, flies on the face + father and uncle blind + follicles and scarring under the upper lid + inturned eyelashes
highlight: repeated episodes of red, itchy, watery eyes
father and an uncle have similar eye symptoms and are now blind
pale follicles on the inner surface

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Chronic follicular conjunctivitis. The clincher: **recurrent follicular conjunctivitis in a child from an endemic region, with relatives blinded by it**.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.a: Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars A, B, Ba and C)
nodes.note: An obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot make its own adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The infectious elementary body enters the cell and becomes a reticulate body that divides; Giemsa stain shows inclusions in conjunctival cells.

nodes.q: How is it passed from child to child?
nodes.a: By eye-seeking flies, hands and shared cloths
nodes.note: Crowding and poor access to water keep the cycle going.

nodes.q: Scarring has rolled his upper lid inward. What is the term for his eyelashes rubbing on the eye?
nodes.note: Repeated infections cause chronic inflammation and scarring of the upper lid conjunctiva, which turns the lid inward (entropion). The lashes scrape the cornea, causing ulcers and opacity.

nodes.q: What is the end result?
nodes.note: Trachoma is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide.

nodes.q: Which drug is given to the patient and to the community?
nodes.note: Part of the SAFE plan: Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement. Macrolides block the 50S ribosome.

nodes.q: Red watery eyes could suggest adenoviral conjunctivitis. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both give red eyes and follicles.

split.note: **Acute onset, tender preauricular node, outbreaks (swimming pools)**; resolves in 2 to 3 weeks without scarring
**Recurrent over years + upper lid scarring + inturned lashes + endemic region**

nodes.q: Other causes of red eyes were possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: Gonococcal conjunctivitis
**Hyperacute thick pus within days, in a newborn or sexually active adult; gram-negative diplococci**
His disease is chronic and watery, without pus
Herpes simplex keratitis
**Painful eye, usually one side; dendritic ulcer on fluorescein staining**
Both eyes, follicles and lid scarring
Bacterial conjunctivitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
**Acute purulent discharge, often both eyes, clears in days**
Years of recurrence, no pus

nodes.q: The same genus causes genital infection and newborn eye disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sexually active adults, or newborns 5 to 14 days old**; also genital infection and pneumonia in infants
**Endemic childhood disease with fly spread and blinding scars**

root.stem: A 29-year-old man has had 3 days of high fever, severe headache and back pain. A rash then appeared on his face and forearms and spread to the trunk and legs, with more lesions on the face and limbs than on the trunk. Every lesion is a firm, deep-seated pustule at the same stage of development. He has no swollen lymph nodes. He attended a crowded public event 12 days ago, where a biological attack is suspected.
root.oneliner: 29M + 3 days of high fever, severe headache, backache + rash starting on face and forearms, denser on face and limbs than trunk + all lesions deep firm pustules at the same stage + no lymphadenopathy + crowded event 12 days ago, suspected bioterrorism
highlight: more lesions on the face and limbs than on the trunk
firm, deep-seated pustule at the same stage of development

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A highly contagious poxvirus disease, eradicated in nature in 1980. The clincher: **centrifugal rash (more on the face and limbs) with all lesions at the same stage**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which type of virus causes it?
nodes.a: A large enveloped DNA poxvirus (variola virus)
nodes.note: It replicates in the cytoplasm using its own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Cytoplasmic inclusions are called Guarnieri bodies.

nodes.q: How does it spread between people?
nodes.a: By respiratory droplets (and contact with lesions)
nodes.note: Humans are the only reservoir, which is why eradication worked. Patients need airborne isolation.

nodes.q: What do the lesions pass through in order?
nodes.note: Scabs leave pitted scars; the face is worst. Death or blindness can follow severe cases.

nodes.q: Which preventive measure, given to his contacts, best controls the outbreak?
nodes.note: Vaccinia is a related live poxvirus that gives cross-immunity. It protects even when given up to about 3 to 4 days after exposure. Ring vaccination of contacts plus isolation of cases controls spread. Immune globulin, acyclovir, amantadine, ribavirin and interleukin-2 do not.

nodes.q: Acyclovir, amantadine and ribavirin do not help here. Which antiviral blocks release of poxvirus particles from infected cells?
nodes.note: It inhibits the viral envelope protein p37 so that virions cannot leave the cell. Brincidofovir (an oral prodrug of cidofovir) is also approved. Acyclovir works on herpes viruses and amantadine on influenza A.

nodes.q: His pustular rash could suggest chickenpox. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both are vesicular or pustular and spread by droplets.

split.note: **Centripetal rash (trunk more than limbs); lesions at different stages (macules, vesicles, crusts together)**; mild illness
**Centrifugal rash with all lesions at the same stage + severe prodrome**

nodes.q: Could this be mpox (monkeypox)? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Similar lesions, but **tender swollen lymph nodes**; milder; zoonotic from African rodents, now also spread by close sexual contact
**No lymphadenopathy**, higher mortality, human-only disease

root.stem: A 27-year-old marine returned from a deployment in Saudi Arabia. Three weeks after an itchy bite from a small night-biting fly on his forearm, which left a skin ulcer, he developed fever, fatigue, pallor and enlarged lymph nodes, and his spleen is palpable. Blood cultures are negative and a blood smear shows no parasites inside red cells. A biopsy of the skin lesion shows enlarged macrophages packed with small intracellular organisms.
root.oneliner: 27M + marine deployed in Saudi Arabia + skin ulcer at an itchy night-fly bite + then fever, fatigue, pallor, adenopathy, splenomegaly + negative blood cultures + smear without red-cell parasites + biopsy: macrophages packed with intracellular organisms
highlight: blood smear shows no parasites inside red cells
macrophages packed with small intracellular organisms

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A protozoal infection that has spread from a skin ulcer to the internal organs. The clincher: **macrophages packed with small intracellular organisms after a biting-fly skin ulcer in an endemic area**.

nodes.q: Which insect transmits it?
nodes.note: Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World. The fly passes flagellated promastigotes, which become amastigotes inside macrophages.

nodes.q: Which organism most likely caused his illness, given the Middle East deployment?
nodes.note: An Old World species usually causing skin ulcers, but it spread to the organs in soldiers during the Gulf War. Leishmania donovani causes classic visceral disease (kala-azar); Leishmania braziliensis causes mucocutaneous disease in the New World.

nodes.q: His pallor and big spleen come from the parasites filling macrophages in which organ system?
nodes.a: The reticuloendothelial system: spleen, liver and bone marrow
nodes.note: The intracellular forms are amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies on Giemsa stain). Marrow involvement gives anemia and pancytopenia; the spleen swells.

nodes.q: What happens if this visceral form goes untreated?
nodes.note: Massive spleen enlargement, high gamma-globulins and darkening skin (kala-azar means black fever). It is fatal in nearly all untreated cases.

nodes.q: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
nodes.a: Seeing amastigotes in a biopsy or aspirate (skin, bone marrow or spleen)
nodes.note: Polymerase chain reaction and serology help. Blood cultures are negative, as in his case.

nodes.q: Which drug treats visceral disease?
nodes.note: Alternatives: pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate) and oral miltefosine.

nodes.q: Fever, anemia and an enlarged spleen after travel could suggest malaria. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both give fever, anemia and splenomegaly in a traveller.

split.note: **Periodic fever and parasites inside red blood cells on the smear**; no skin ulcer or macrophage organisms
**Sand fly bite ulcer + organisms inside macrophages + no red-cell parasites**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A tick-borne spirochete infection. The clincher: **an expanding ring-shaped red rash with central clearing after a summer stay in New England, followed weeks later by migratory joint swelling, facial palsy and heart block**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: What is the name of the early rash?
nodes.note: The exam may call it erythema chronicum migrans, the older name. It expands over days (**at least 5 cm**), often clears centrally, and is itself enough to diagnose early Lyme disease; it is not itchy or painful.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A spirochete: a thin, spiral-shaped bacterium with a weakly gram-negative envelope. Unlike Treponema it is large enough to see with Giemsa or Wright stain; it grows only in special media (**Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly medium**), so cultures are rarely used. The white-footed mouse is the main reservoir and white-tailed deer keep the tick population going.

nodes.q: Which tick carries it?
nodes.note: The same tick also carries Babesia and Anaplasma, so co-infection is possible. The tick usually has to stay attached for 36 to 48 hours to pass on the organism, so most patients never notice the bite.

nodes.q: Which infection, spread by water contaminated with animal urine, is caused by a spiral-shaped relative of this organism?
nodes.note: Leptospira is also a spirochete (a tightly coiled spiral with hooked ends). The three spirochete genera are Borrelia, Leptospira and Treponema (syphilis). Leptospirosis gives fever, conjunctival suffusion and, in severe cases, jaundice with kidney failure (Weil disease).

nodes.q: Which nerve is affected to cause his facial droop?
nodes.note: The most common neurologic sign of early disseminated disease; it can be bilateral, which is a strong clue to Lyme disease over Bell palsy. Lymphocytic meningitis and painful radiculopathy can also occur at this stage.

nodes.q: Which conduction problem explains his fainting after a pounding heartbeat?
nodes.note: Lyme carditis: the PR interval lengthens and the block can swing quickly between first degree and complete heart block. Complete block can cause sudden death, so these patients are admitted and monitored; it usually resolves with antibiotics, sometimes with a temporary pacemaker.

nodes.q: Which joint is most often affected in Lyme arthritis?
nodes.note: Large-joint oligoarthritis, migratory early on and then lasting weeks in one knee at a time if untreated. Joint fluid is inflammatory and does not grow bacteria on routine culture.

nodes.q: Months to years after untreated infection, which problem causes poor memory, low mood and insomnia?
nodes.note: Months to years later the symptoms wax and wane: poor memory, low mood, insomnia, fatigue and joint pain in someone who once had erythema migrans. Late disease also includes chronic knee arthritis and peripheral neuropathy; the old rash is the key clue.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis after the rash has faded?

nodes.note: Two-tier testing: a screening enzyme immunoassay, then a Western blot (or a second enzyme immunoassay). nodes.q: Which antibiotic treats early Lyme disease in a teenager?
nodes.note: Amoxicillin or cefuroxime in pregnancy. Short doxycycline courses (21 days or less) are now considered safe at any age, but exam questions may still prefer amoxicillin under age 8. nodes.q: Which step of protein synthesis does doxycycline block?

nodes.q: Why is doxycycline avoided in pregnancy?

nodes.note: It binds calcium and deposits in developing bones and teeth, causing yellow-brown tooth discoloration and possibly impaired bone growth. Other effects: photosensitivity and pill esophagitis. Absorption falls when taken with milk, antacids or iron.

nodes.note: The tube is short, narrow and horizontal in young children, so it drains poorly. The middle ear is separated from the throat only by this tube; the inner ear is not reached.

nodes.q: Which organism most often causes it?
nodes.note: Next are nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. Haemophilus and Moraxella can make beta-lactamase, which is why amoxicillin fails in some children. A viral cold usually comes first.

nodes.q: Which serovars cause genital infection?

nodes.q: Which organism is the most likely cause?

nodes.q: Which blood culture finding supports the catheter as the source?

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Invasive intestinal infection, with possible spread to the liver. The clincher: **fever and bloody, mucus-streaked stools from a tropical region with flask-shaped colonic ulcers and right upper quadrant tenderness**.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?

nodes.q: Which drug kills the tissue-invading trophozoites?

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Sepsis (infection with a body-wide inflammatory response) with low blood pressure that fluids do not correct and a raised lactate. The clincher: **low blood pressure unresponsive to fluids + warm flushed skin + low systemic vascular resistance with high cardiac output + a positive blood culture**. In the elderly the temperature may be low and confusion may be the only early sign.

nodes.q: Which category of shock is this?
nodes.note: Blood vessels dilate, so the blood pressure falls although the heart pumps well. Anaphylactic and neurogenic shock are also distributive.

nodes.q: His cardiac output is high now. If the shock goes untreated for days, which way does the cardiac output move?
nodes.note: Early on, the low systemic vascular resistance (low afterload) and the sympathetic drive raise the output, and the wedge pressure is low or normal. Later, cytokines depress the heart muscle and fluid leaks out of the vessels, so the output falls and the skin turns cold. In hemorrhagic shock the output is low and the resistance high from the start.

nodes.q: Which part of the gram-negative cell wall acts as the endotoxin that triggers the response?
nodes.note: Lipid A binds CD14 and Toll-like receptor 4 on macrophages. The O antigen (the long polysaccharide chains) varies between strains and is not the toxic part; capsule resists phagocytosis, fimbriae help attachment, and porins let molecules through the outer membrane.

nodes.q: Which macrophage cytokine is the key early mediator that starts the cascade?
nodes.note: Interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 add to it; together they cause fever, vasodilation, capillary leak and the liver's acute-phase response (C-reactive protein is a product of that response, not a starter). nodes.q: Which consumptive clotting disorder is the key blood complication of his sepsis?
nodes.note: Endotoxin and cytokines turn on tissue factor and the clotting cascade. Platelets and clotting factors are used up, so there are small clots in the vessels and bleeding from puncture sites.

nodes.q: Which lung complication follows widespread capillary leak?
nodes.note: Damaged alveolar capillaries leak protein-rich fluid into the alveoli, causing hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates and a normal wedge pressure.

nodes.q: What is the final common cause of death?
nodes.note: Poor tissue perfusion with microthrombi injures the kidneys (acute tubular necrosis), liver, brain and heart. Lactic acidosis reflects tissue hypoxia.

nodes.q: Which blood test shows tissue hypoperfusion and guides resuscitation?
nodes.note: A level above 2 mmol/L signals hypoperfusion; above 4 mmol/L, as here, calls for fluids at once. Blood cultures are drawn before antibiotics, but antibiotics must not wait for the results.

nodes.q: What is the first treatment for the low blood pressure?

nodes.q: How soon after recognition should broad-spectrum antibiotics be given?

nodes.note: It acts on alpha-1 receptors to constrict vessels and on beta-1 receptors to support the heart.

nodes.q: Which second vasopressor, one that does not act on adrenergic receptors, is added if the pressure stays low on norepinephrine?
nodes.note: Vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) acts on V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle (Gq pathway, more intracellular calcium), constricting vessels independently of adrenergic receptors.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mild childhood viral illness. The clincher: **bright red cheeks followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs**, after a mild cold-like illness.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?

nodes.q: Which virus causes it?

nodes.q: Which cells does the virus infect?

nodes.note: The virus kills these dividing precursors, so red cell production stops and the reticulocyte count falls.

nodes.q: Which red cell surface antigen does the virus use as its receptor?
nodes.note: People who lack P antigen are resistant to infection.

nodes.q: What is the cause of her anemia?
nodes.note: Red cells live 120 days, so a healthy child loses little hemoglobin and has only a mild, transient drop.

nodes.q: In which patients does this become a severe transient aplastic crisis?

nodes.note: Red cells in these patients live only days, so a pause in production causes severe anemia with a near-zero reticulocyte count.

nodes.q: Infection of a pregnant woman can cause which condition in the fetus?

nodes.q: Why is a child no longer contagious once the rash appears?

nodes.q: If her mother catches the virus, which joint problem is typical?

nodes.note: Immune-complex arthritis in adults, mostly women; it mimics rheumatoid arthritis but settles in weeks. Adults often have no rash.

nodes.q: Which test confirms a recent infection?
nodes.note: In immunocompromised patients and in aplastic crisis, polymerase chain reaction of the blood is used because antibodies may be absent. Treatment is supportive; transfuse in aplastic crisis and give intravenous immunoglobulin in chronic infection.

nodes.q: Anemia after a viral illness could suggest autoimmune hemolytic anemia. How do you tell them apart?

**Low reticulocyte count + slapped cheeks + lacy rash**; Coombs test negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mold infection of the lungs that invades blood vessels in the immunocompromised. The clincher: **prolonged neutropenia + fever despite antibiotics + nodules or a cavity with a surrounding halo + a positive serum fungal antigen**.

nodes.q: What does a lung biopsy of the mold show?
nodes.a: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles (about 45 degrees)
nodes.note: Aspergillus fumigatus; seen on silver (Gomori methenamine) or periodic acid-Schiff stains. The spores are inhaled.

nodes.q: The positive serum test most likely detects which component?
nodes.a: Galactomannan, a polysaccharide of the fungal cell wall
nodes.note: Galactomannan is part of the cell wall, not of flagella, spores or ribosomes. Beta-D-glucan is another cell wall component; it is also positive in Candida and Pneumocystis, but not in Mucor or Cryptococcus. The test is also done on bronchoalveolar lavage.

nodes.q: Which host defect makes inhaled spores dangerous?
nodes.a: Neutropenia, which removes the main defense against the hyphae
nodes.note: Macrophages kill spores and neutrophils kill hyphae. Corticosteroids and graft-versus-host disease add risk.

nodes.q: Which inherited phagocyte disorder also predisposes to it?
nodes.note: Lack of NADPH oxidase prevents the respiratory burst, so catalase-positive organisms such as Aspergillus and Staphylococcus aureus survive. The dihydrorhodamine test shows it.

nodes.q: What causes the ring of ground-glass opacity around his nodules?
nodes.a: Hemorrhage around the nodule from angioinvasion (the halo sign)
nodes.note: The mold invades vessels, causing thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarcts. Later, as neutrophils recover, the necrotic center retracts and leaves an air crescent around the nodule.

nodes.q: Which fatal complication follows erosion into a pulmonary artery?
nodes.note: The fungus can also spread through blood to the brain, causing abscesses and hemorrhage.

nodes.q: What establishes the diagnosis with certainty?
nodes.a: Biopsy showing septate hyphae invading tissue, with culture
nodes.note: Computed tomography of the chest and galactomannan in serum or bronchoalveolar lavage are used first and treatment starts on a probable diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line?
nodes.a: Voriconazole (isavuconazole is an equal first choice)
nodes.note: Amphotericin B and echinocandins are alternatives.

nodes.q: How does it kill the fungus?
nodes.a: It inhibits the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis
nodes.note: Side effects are hepatotoxicity, visual disturbances and many drug interactions through cytochrome P450 inhibition. Echinocandins block beta-1,3-glucan synthase in the cell wall.

nodes.q: A cavitary lung lesion in a neutropenic patient could suggest mucormycosis. How do you tell them apart?

**Septate hyphae at acute angles + positive galactomannan + lung nodules with halo**; no sinus involvement

swelling around both eyes and tender muscles

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A roundworm infection acquired from undercooked meat. The clincher: **fever, severe myalgias and periorbital edema with eosinophilia and high creatine kinase after eating undercooked meat**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A nematode (roundworm). Pork, bear, walrus and wild boar carry the larvae in their muscle. In Arctic game such as bear the species is often Trichinella nativa, which resists freezing.

nodes.q: Where do the larvae encyst in the human host?
nodes.a: In striated (skeletal) muscle cells, forming nurse cells
nodes.note: Ingested larvae mature to adults in the small intestine (diarrhea and abdominal pain in the first week). Adult females release new larvae that travel in blood to muscle, causing fever, myalgia and eosinophilia in weeks 2 to 3.

nodes.q: Which muscles do the larvae favour, explaining his jaw pain?
nodes.a: Very active, well-perfused striated muscles: the masseters, tongue, diaphragm and extraocular muscles
nodes.note: Involvement of the diaphragm causes trouble breathing. The swelling around the eyes comes from the immune reaction (allergic vasculitis and capillary leak) with extraocular myositis.

nodes.q: Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Muscle biopsy showing encysted coiled larvae
nodes.note: A high eosinophil count supports the diagnosis but does not establish it. Serology (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) turns positive after 3 to 5 weeks. Stool examination for ova or Gram stain is negative because the larvae live in muscle; plain radiographs show nothing until the cysts calcify.

nodes.q: Which drug kills the worms?

nodes.note: They bind beta-tubulin, blocking microtubule polymerization and glucose uptake. Steroids dampen the inflammatory reaction.

nodes.q: Which complication is the most common cause of death?
nodes.note: Larval invasion of the heart causes inflammation without encystment, leading to arrhythmia and heart failure. Encephalitis and pneumonitis are other serious complications.

nodes.q: Months later, what happens to the cysts?
nodes.note: Muscle pain may persist for months after treatment.

nodes.q: What cooking temperature prevents it?
nodes.a: Cook meat to an internal temperature of 71°C (160°F)
nodes.note: Freezing is unreliable for wild game because arctic strains resist it.

nodes.q: Swelling around the eyes and muscle pain could suggest dermatomyositis. How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the clinic alone because of 3 days of thick yellow vaginal discharge and burning with urination, and she asks that her parents not be told she is sexually active. There are no external genital lesions, the vaginal walls look normal, pus is seen at the cervical os, and the cervix bleeds easily when touched. migrating pains in her wrists and knees
The right knee is hot and swollen
pus is seen at the cervical os

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A sexually transmitted infection of mucosal surfaces. The clincher: **purulent discharge with gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils** on Gram stain.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus with no capsule. It grows on Thayer-Martin medium and ferments glucose only (the meningococcus ferments glucose and maltose).

nodes.q: Which surface structure lets it attach to the cells lining the genital tract?
nodes.note: The pilus protein is the main antigen the host mounts an antibody response against.

nodes.q: How does the organism escape the antibodies made against that structure?
nodes.a: Antigenic variation by gene recombination, so the pilus keeps changing
nodes.note: This is why past infection gives little protection and no vaccine exists. It also makes an IgA protease that cuts mucosal IgA, and Opa proteins that help it stick.

nodes.q: An experimental gonococcal vaccine given as a nasal spray raises antibodies in vaginal secretions. How do the antibodies get there?
nodes.a: IgA-producing B cells primed in the airway mucosa travel to seed all mucosal sites
nodes.note: The common mucosal immune system: B cells activated at one mucosal surface home to other mucosal tissues and secrete IgA there. Circulating IgG made after a skin or muscle injection does not do this.

nodes.q: Which complication follows when the infection climbs from the cervix?
nodes.note: Fever, lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness; it can spread to the liver capsule (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

nodes.q: Which long-term tubal change causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy?
nodes.note: Scarring of the fallopian tube damages the cilia and narrows the lumen, so the egg is not carried properly.

nodes.q: What explains her fever, joint pains, hot knee and pustules?
nodes.a: Spread of the bacteria through the blood (disseminated gonococcal infection)
nodes.note: The arthritis-dermatitis syndrome: **migratory joint pains or tenosynovitis + a few painful necrotic pustules + fever**. It is more common in women during menstruation or pregnancy; the joint fluid Gram stain and culture are often negative, so culture the cervix, urethra, rectum and throat. Gonorrhea is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults.

nodes.q: Which inherited defect makes repeated Neisseria bloodstream infections likely?
nodes.note: The membrane attack complex is needed to lyse Neisseria, so repeated meningococcal or disseminated gonococcal infections should prompt a total hemolytic complement (CH50) test.

nodes.q: Which test confirms infection and also detects a second organism in the same sample?
nodes.a: Nucleic acid amplification test of a urine sample or swab
nodes.note: Culture on Thayer-Martin medium is kept for antibiotic susceptibility testing and for joint fluid or blood. A Gram stain showing intracellular diplococci is enough to start treatment.

nodes.q: Which antibiotic is the treatment?
nodes.note: Uncomplicated cervicitis or urethritis: one intramuscular dose. Disseminated infection, as in her case: ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously daily, usually in hospital, with drainage of a septic joint. Add doxycycline when chlamydia has not been excluded. Treat the partner as well. Fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread.

nodes.q: How does the drug kill the organism?
nodes.a: It binds penicillin-binding proteins and blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking
nodes.note: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin; it is bactericidal and works on the cell wall.

nodes.q: She is 17, the Gram stain already shows the organism, and she asks that her parents not be told. What is the right course?
nodes.a: Treat her now without notifying her parents
nodes.note: Minors can consent to testing and treatment of sexually transmitted infections in every US state. Do not wait for the test results, and do not ask a parent or sibling for consent. Encourage, but do not force, communication with a trusted adult.

nodes.q: After treatment is started, which step comes next?
nodes.a: Counsel her and test for other sexually transmitted infections such as HIV and syphilis
nodes.note: Also offer chlamydia testing if not done, report the case to the health department, arrange partner treatment (expedited partner therapy where allowed) and retest in 3 months. It is not the doctor's place to interview the partners directly.

nodes.q: Which eye disease can appear in a newborn born to an infected mother?
nodes.a: Gonococcal conjunctivitis of the newborn (ophthalmia neonatorum), 2 to 5 days after birth
nodes.note: Purulent conjunctivitis that can perforate the cornea; prevented by erythromycin ointment at birth. Chlamydial conjunctivitis appears later, at 5 to 14 days.

nodes.q: What does the infection cause in her partner's scrotum?
nodes.note: Pain is relieved when the scrotum is lifted (positive Prehn sign), unlike testicular torsion. In sexually active men under 35 the usual causes are gonorrhea and chlamydia; in older men and men who have insertive anal sex, enteric gram-negative rods.

root.stem: A 24-year-old man develops sudden, profuse watery diarrhea 2 days after returning from relief work at a flooded refugee camp. He passes about 1 liter per hour of pale, cloudy stool flecked with mucus and smelling of fish, with no blood, no abdominal pain and no fever. nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A secretory diarrhea. The clincher: **profuse painless watery diarrhea like rice water, with no blood and no fever**, after exposure to contaminated water.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A comma-shaped gram-negative rod with one polar flagellum (darting motility), oxidase positive. It grows in alkaline media and on TCBS agar as yellow colonies. It stays in the gut lumen and does not invade.

nodes.q: Which G protein does its toxin lock in the active state?
nodes.a: The stimulatory G protein (Gs), by ADP-ribosylation
nodes.note: The A subunit of cholera toxin does this; the B subunits bind GM1 ganglioside on the enterocyte. Pertussis toxin, by contrast, ADP-ribosylates and disables the inhibitory G protein (Gi).

nodes.q: What happens next inside the intestinal cell?
nodes.a: Cyclic AMP rises and the chloride channel (CFTR) stays open, so chloride, sodium and water pour into the lumen
nodes.note: The loss is of isotonic fluid; the epithelium itself is not destroyed, which is why there is no blood or fever.

nodes.q: Which acid-base disturbance results from the stool losses?
nodes.note: Bicarbonate is lost in the stool and chloride is retained, so the anion gap stays normal (136 - 114 - 12 = 10). Potassium is lost too, so hypokalemia follows.

nodes.q: Why does oral glucose-and-salt solution work even though secretion continues?
nodes.a: Sodium-glucose cotransport (SGLT1) in the brush border is still intact, so glucose pulls sodium and water in
nodes.note: Cholera toxin does not damage this transporter. Rice-based solutions work the same way.

nodes.q: What is the treatment priority?
nodes.a: Fluid and electrolyte replacement: oral rehydration, with intravenous fluids if severe
nodes.note: Lactated Ringer solution for shock; a single dose of doxycycline or azithromycin shortens the illness. Antidiarrheals are not the key.

nodes.q: Why does an injected killed whole-cell vaccine protect poorly?
nodes.a: It does not induce secretory IgA at the intestinal surface
nodes.note: The organism stays on the mucosa, where only secretory IgA can reach it. Circulating IgG does not get into the lumen. Oral vaccines work better.

nodes.q: His diarrhea could suggest enterotoxigenic E. coli. How do you tell them apart?

**Rice-water stool at a liter per hour with shock and a non-gap acidosis**, often in outbreaks after floods

nodes.note: The trap: the heat-labile toxin of E. coli works almost exactly like cholera toxin.

nodes.q: Watery diarrhea without blood could suggest rotavirus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually a child under 2; **fever and vomiting first, then watery diarrhea**; villous damage causes malabsorption
**An adult with a liter an hour of rice-water stool, no fever, and intact villi**

nodes.q: His fever, fast pulse, soft blood pressure and flushed skin could suggest toxic shock syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tampon, wound or nasal packing source + diffuse sunburn-like rash + low blood pressure + multi-organ dysfunction** from a Staphylococcus aureus superantigen toxin; peeling of palms and soles 1 to 2 weeks later
**Begins hours after the first antibiotic dose for a spirochete infection, resolves in 24 hours, no organ failure**, even in a menstruating woman using a tampon

nodes.note: Both give fever, a fast pulse and flushing; a tampon in the history is a deliberate distractor.

nodes.q: His fever, chills and fast pulse could suggest sepsis from the infection itself. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Organ dysfunction (confusion, low urine output, rising lactate) from an uncontrolled infection**, worsening over hours to days despite treatment
**Starts hours after the first antibiotic dose and settles within 24 hours** with supportive care while the same antibiotic continues

nodes.note: Spirochete infections such as syphilis and early Lyme disease rarely cause sepsis.

nodes.q: A reaction soon after a drug could suggest drug-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bleeding, petechiae, low platelets, prolonged prothrombin time and raised D-dimer**
**No bleeding or clotting abnormality**; fever, chills and myalgias that resolve within a day

nodes.q: His new fever could suggest antibiotic resistance. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever persists or returns days after starting the drug and nothing improves**; Treponema pallidum has no penicillin resistance
**New fever within hours of the first dose that clears on its own** while the infection is being killed

root.stem: A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of sudden fever, chills, headache and weakness. Five days ago he finished a camping trip in New Mexico, where he slept near a prairie dog colony and noticed small itchy bites on his right leg. His temperature is 39.8°C and his pulse is 118/min. A very tender, swollen, matted mass 5 cm wide is felt in his right groin, with warm red skin over it and a small healing bite on the leg below. Gram stain of fluid aspirated from the mass shows gram-negative coccobacilli, and a Wright-Giemsa stain shows them darker at both ends, like a safety pin.
root.oneliner: 26M + sudden fever, chills, headache + camping in New Mexico near a prairie dog colony + itchy bites on right leg + very tender matted right groin mass + gram-negative coccobacilli with safety-pin bipolar staining
highlight: sudden fever, chills, headache and weakness
small itchy bites on his right leg
darker at both ends, like a safety pin

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection of a lymph node after a flea bite; the swollen node is called a bubo. The clincher: **a very tender, matted bubo after rodent and flea exposure in the American Southwest, with gram-negative coccobacilli showing bipolar safety-pin staining**.

nodes.q: Which organism is the cause?
nodes.note: A gram-negative coccobacillus that stains darker at both ends (bipolar, safety-pin). Virulence factors include the F1 capsule and Yersinia outer proteins injected by a type III secretion system.

nodes.q: Which insect most likely carried the bacteria from the rodents to him?
nodes.a: Fleas (classically the rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis)
nodes.note: Bacteria block the flea's gut and are regurgitated into the bite. Reservoirs are wild rodents such as prairie dogs, ground squirrels and rats; most US cases are in New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and California.

nodes.q: Why is the node in the groin involved?
nodes.a: It drains the lymphatics of the bitten leg
nodes.note: The bacteria travel to the regional node, which becomes swollen, hemorrhagic and necrotic.

nodes.q: Which complication follows spread into the blood?
nodes.note: Shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with gangrene of the fingers and toes, which gave the Black Death its name.

nodes.q: Which form spreads person to person through respiratory droplets?
nodes.note: Spread to the lungs gives a severe pneumonia with bloody sputum; it is the deadliest form, is always fatal untreated, and is the form feared in bioterrorism (aerosol).

nodes.q: Who needs antibiotic prophylaxis and isolation measures?
nodes.a: Close contacts of a pneumonic plague patient (doxycycline); the patient needs droplet precautions
nodes.note: Pneumonic plague patients stay in droplet isolation until 48 hours of effective therapy.

nodes.q: What is the first-line treatment?
nodes.note: Start on clinical suspicion without waiting for culture. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) or doxycycline are alternatives.

nodes.q: How do aminoglycosides kill bacteria?
nodes.a: They bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause misreading of messenger RNA, which is bactericidal
nodes.note: They block the initiation complex and cause misreading. Uptake needs oxygen-dependent transport, so they do not work on anaerobes. Toxicities: kidney damage and hearing or balance loss.

nodes.q: A tender node after camping could suggest tularemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rabbit, tick or deer-fly exposure + skin ulcer with regional nodes** (ulceroglandular), more common in the south-central US (Arkansas, Missouri); Francisella tularensis, a small gram-negative coccobacillus that needs cysteine to grow
**Flea bite or rodent exposure in the Southwest + very tender bubo without a skin ulcer + bipolar safety-pin staining**

nodes.note: The trap: both are zoonotic gram-negative coccobacilli that respond to aminoglycosides.

nodes.q: A tender node after an animal exposure could suggest cat-scratch disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Kitten scratch or bite + papule at the site + regional node weeks later, mild illness**; Bartonella henselae seen on Warthin-Starry silver stain
**Sudden high fever and toxicity with a very tender, matted bubo after flea exposure**

nodes.q: A bite on the leg with a swollen node could suggest cutaneous anthrax. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless black eschar with surrounding edema**; gram-positive spore-forming rods in chains
**Exquisitely tender bubo, gram-negative coccobacilli, no eschar**

nodes.q: His fever and chills after travel could suggest malaria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Travel to a tropical region + cyclic fever + ring forms inside red blood cells**; no lymph node mass
**Tender bubo + gram-negative coccobacilli in the node aspirate** after rodent and flea exposure in the Southwest

root.stem: A 31-year-old man who moved 2 years ago from a rural village in Peru, where pigs roamed freely near his home, has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. For 5 weeks he has had morning headaches and vomiting. He is afebrile, a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test is negative, and a relative who lived with him passed white rice-like segments in stool. Fundoscopy shows swelling of both optic discs. Head computed tomography shows several small calcified nodules in the brain tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows several small cysts, one with a bright dot inside, and a cyst inside the left lateral ventricle at its outlet, with an enlarged left lateral ventricle; the right lateral, third and fourth ventricles are normal.
root.oneliner: 31M + moved from rural Peru with free-roaming pigs + first generalized seizure + 5 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting + bilateral papilledema + calcified nodules and cysts with a dot + cyst at the outlet of an enlarged left lateral ventricle, other ventricles normal
highlight: passed white rice-like segments in stool
one with a bright dot inside
cyst inside the left lateral ventricle at its outlet
right lateral, third and fourth ventricles are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection of the brain by the larval cysts of the pork tapeworm. The clincher: **cystic brain lesions, one with a dot (the scolex), plus calcified nodules in a person from an endemic area who presents with seizures**.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: The larvae (cysticerci) each have a single head, the scolex, seen as the bright dot inside the cyst.

nodes.q: How does a person get the brain cysts?
nodes.a: By swallowing Taenia solium eggs passed in the stool of a tapeworm carrier (fecal-oral)
nodes.note: Eggs hatch in the gut, larvae cross the wall and spread in the blood to brain, muscle and eye. Eating undercooked pork gives an intestinal tapeworm, not brain cysts; the relative with segments in the stool was the source.

nodes.q: Neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of which acquired neurologic condition worldwide?
nodes.note: Seizures are the most frequent presentation; the cysts irritate cortex as they die.

nodes.q: What do the calcified nodules on imaging represent?
nodes.note: Cysts pass through vesicular (live, no inflammation), colloidal (dying, ring-enhancing with edema), granular and calcified stages. Calcified nodules can still provoke seizures.

nodes.q: Why is only the left lateral ventricle enlarged?
nodes.a: The cyst blocks the left interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro), causing obstructive hydrocephalus
nodes.note: The foramen of Monro connects each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. A cyst in the cerebral aqueduct would enlarge both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle; cysts in the basal cisterns block cerebrospinal fluid absorption and cause communicating hydrocephalus.

nodes.q: Which finding on his eye examination shows the raised intracranial pressure?
nodes.note: Morning headache and vomiting come from the same cause.

nodes.q: Which complication could a lumbar puncture cause before this is treated?
nodes.note: Obstructive hydrocephalus raises pressure above the block; image first.

nodes.q: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
nodes.a: MRI showing a cyst with a scolex, supported by serum enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) for anticysticercal antibodies
nodes.note: MRI is more sensitive than CT for the scolex and for small intraventricular cysts.

nodes.q: What is done first for the blocked foramen?
nodes.a: Neurosurgical relief: endoscopic cyst removal or a ventricular shunt
nodes.note: Antiparasitic drugs are given only after pressure is controlled, because dying larvae swell.

nodes.q: Which drug kills viable cysts, and what is given with it?
nodes.a: Albendazole with a corticosteroid; antiseizure drugs for seizures
nodes.note: Steroids blunt the inflammation from dying larvae. Praziquantel can be added. Antiparasitic drugs are not given when only calcified (dead) lesions are present.

nodes.q: How does albendazole work?
nodes.a: It binds parasite beta-tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization
nodes.note: Praziquantel instead raises calcium permeability and causes paralysis of the worm.

nodes.q: Ring-enhancing brain lesions with seizures could suggest a tuberculoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tuberculosis exposure or lung disease + a solid caseating granuloma with basal meningeal enhancement**; no scolex
**Cysts with a scolex dot + calcified nodules + tapeworm carrier in the household**

nodes.note: The trap: both are ring-enhancing lesions that cause seizures in immigrants from endemic regions.

nodes.q: Ring-enhancing lesions could suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **HIV with a CD4 count below 100 + multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia**; treated with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine
**HIV-negative + cysts with a scolex + calcified nodules** from an endemic area

nodes.q: A cystic brain mass with seizures could suggest a brain abscess. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, a single ring-enhancing lesion with restricted diffusion, and a source such as sinusitis or endocarditis**
**Afebrile, multiple cysts of different ages, a scolex dot and calcified nodules**

nodes.q: Seizures with an abnormal brain image could suggest herpes simplex encephalitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever and confusion over days + temporal lobe involvement + red blood cells in cerebrospinal fluid**; treated with acyclovir
**Afebrile, weeks of raised pressure, scattered cysts with a scolex and calcified nodules**

root.stem: A 28-year-old married man has had 3 days of burning with urination and a thick yellow-white discharge at the tip of his penis. Two weeks ago he had unprotected sex with a new partner at a conference. He has no fever, flank pain or scrotal pain, and his prostate is not tender. Urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no nitrites, and a Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. The next day, his wife telephones the office and asks what he was diagnosed with.
root.oneliner: 28M + 3 days of dysuria and thick purulent urethral discharge + unprotected sex with a new partner 2 weeks ago + afebrile, no flank or scrotal pain, non-tender prostate + white cells, no nitrites + intracellular gram-negative diplococci + wife calls asking about his diagnosis
highlight: burning with urination and a thick yellow-white discharge
unprotected sex with a new partner
no fever, flank pain or scrotal pain

nodes.q: Which syndrome does he have?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the urethra, usually from a sexually transmitted infection. The clincher: **dysuria with a purulent urethral discharge and white cells but no nitrites after a new sexual partner**.

nodes.q: Which organism does the Gram stain show?
nodes.note: Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils; oxidase-positive, grown on Thayer-Martin medium. Pilus antigenic variation and IgA protease explain why infection does not give lasting immunity.

nodes.q: Which second organism often co-infects and is the leading bacterial cause of non-gonococcal urethritis?
nodes.note: An obligate intracellular bacterium (elementary body enters, reticulate body replicates); it is not seen on Gram stain and is found by nucleic acid testing.

nodes.q: Which complication of spread into the blood gives a few pustules on the hands, inflamed tendon sheaths and joint pain?
nodes.note: Triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis (painful pustules on an erythematous base) and polyarthralgia; it can settle into one joint as a purulent septic arthritis, the commonest septic arthritis in sexually active young adults.

nodes.q: Which joint infection can it localize to, most often in the knee?
nodes.note: Synovial fluid with more than 50,000 white cells per microliter, mostly neutrophils; treated with intravenous ceftriaxone.

nodes.q: Recurrent disseminated Neisseria infections point to a deficiency of which immune proteins?
nodes.a: Terminal complement components C5 to C9 (membrane attack complex)
nodes.note: Without the membrane attack complex, the thin-walled Neisseria cannot be lysed. Eculizumab, which blocks C5, carries the same risk.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the cause?
nodes.a: Nucleic acid amplification test on first-void urine or a urethral swab
nodes.note: Tests for gonorrhea and chlamydia together; also screen for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis.

nodes.q: What empiric treatment covers both organisms?
nodes.note: Ceftriaxone binds penicillin-binding proteins and blocks cell-wall synthesis; doxycycline binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and covers Chlamydia.

nodes.q: Who else must be treated?
nodes.a: All sexual partners from the previous 60 days
nodes.note: Abstain from sex until 7 days after both he and partners are treated; the infection is reported to public health.

nodes.q: His wife telephones and asks whether he has a sexually transmitted disease. What is the most appropriate response?
nodes.a: Tell her you need her husband's permission before you can discuss his care with her
nodes.note: Confidentiality applies to spouses too, and hinting counts as disclosure: telling her to see her gynecologist or to ask him about relations outside the marriage reveals the diagnosis. Encourage him to tell his wife himself, since she needs treatment; if he refuses, the health department can notify partners without naming him.

nodes.q: Which scrotal complication can follow untreated infection in a young man?
nodes.note: Unilateral scrotal pain with a tender, swollen epididymis; in sexually active men under 35 the cause is usually Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. Pain eases when the testis is lifted, unlike testicular torsion.

nodes.q: Which condition of urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis follows some chlamydial infections, mainly in HLA-B27 carriers?
nodes.note: Formerly called Reiter syndrome; the joint symptoms appear 1 to 4 weeks after the infection.

nodes.q: Which late urethral problem can follow untreated infection?
nodes.note: Scarring narrows the urethra and weakens the urine stream.

nodes.q: Dysuria in a man could suggest a bacterial urinary tract infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Urgency and frequency, positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase, culture grows Escherichia coli**; no urethral discharge; uncommon in young men without a structural problem
**Urethral discharge after a new sexual partner + white cells, no nitrites + diplococci in neutrophils**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause burning with urination and white cells in the urine.

nodes.q: Dysuria with pelvic discomfort could suggest acute prostatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, perineal pain, a tender boggy prostate and obstructive urinary symptoms**; Escherichia coli
**Urethral discharge, afebrile, non-tender prostate**

root.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had 2 days of fever, a throbbing headache, pain when she looks at bright light and a stiff neck. It is August, and her roommate had a similar illness last week. She is alert and fully oriented, with no rash or focal weakness. Lumbar puncture shows a mildly raised opening pressure, 220 white blood cells/mm3 with 90% lymphocytes, glucose 60 mg/dL (serum 95 mg/dL), protein 70 mg/dL, and a negative Gram stain.
root.oneliner: 19F + 2 days of fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness + August with a sick roommate + alert and oriented, no rash or focal signs + cerebrospinal fluid with 90% lymphocytes, normal glucose, mildly high protein, negative Gram stain
highlight: fever, a throbbing headache, pain when she looks at bright light and a stiff neck

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the meninges caused by a virus, usually mild and self-limited. The clincher: **fever, headache and a stiff neck with a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid, normal glucose and a negative Gram stain in a patient with normal mental status**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Meningitis with no bacteria on Gram stain or routine culture; most cases are viral.

nodes.q: Which cerebrospinal fluid pattern points to a viral cause?
nodes.a: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and mildly raised protein
nodes.note: Bacterial meningitis instead gives neutrophils, low glucose and very high protein.

nodes.q: Which group of viruses is the most common cause in all age groups?
nodes.note: Single-stranded positive-sense RNA, non-enveloped picornaviruses spread by the fecal-oral route, with a peak in summer and fall; her sick roommate in August fits.

nodes.q: Which herpesvirus causes recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis (Mollaret)?
nodes.note: Other viral causes include mumps (unvaccinated), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) at seroconversion, and West Nile virus (an arbovirus of late summer).

nodes.q: Which test identifies the virus?
nodes.a: Polymerase chain reaction on cerebrospinal fluid
nodes.note: Enterovirus polymerase chain reaction is fast and sensitive; also check for herpes simplex virus when there is encephalitis.

nodes.q: What is the management in a well-appearing, alert patient?
nodes.a: Supportive care with analgesics, antiemetics and fluids
nodes.note: Acyclovir only if herpes simplex virus is suspected. Give empiric antibiotics while bacterial meningitis is still possible.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.note: Unlike bacterial meningitis, it leaves no hearing loss or other lasting deficits in most patients.

nodes.q: Her fever and stiff neck could suggest bacterial meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Neutrophils in cerebrospinal fluid + low glucose + high protein + organisms on Gram stain**; ill-appearing, may be confused
**Lymphocytes + normal glucose + mildly raised protein + negative Gram stain**; alert, well-appearing, sick contacts in summer

nodes.note: The trap: the headache, fever and stiff neck are identical.

nodes.q: Fever and headache with lymphocytes in the fluid could suggest herpes simplex encephalitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Confusion, seizures or personality change + temporal lobe lesions + red blood cells in cerebrospinal fluid**; needs acyclovir
**Alert and oriented, no focal signs, no temporal lobe changes**

nodes.q: A lymphocytic meningitis could suggest tuberculous meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weeks of illness + low glucose + very high protein + basal meningeal enhancement**; cranial nerve palsies
**Two days of illness + normal glucose + mildly raised protein + full recovery**

nodes.q: A lymphocytic meningitis could suggest cryptococcal meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Advanced HIV or immunosuppression + very high opening pressure + positive cryptococcal antigen or India ink**
**Healthy host + summer exposure + normal glucose + negative cryptococcal antigen**
